passages.happening:
‘That night sleep escaped the king; so he ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles, to be brought in and read to him’ (verse 1). There it is found recorded that Mordecai had exposed the two eunuchs who plotted to kill the king (verse 2).

The king asks, “What honor or dignity has been bestowed on Mordecai for this act?” “Nothing has been done for him,” replied the king’s attendants (verse 3).

“Who is in the court?” the king asked (verse 4). At that very moment Haman has come into the outer court, to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he has prepared. “Bring him in,” ordered the king (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This chapter happens in the single night and morning between Esther's two banquets, and it turns the book around.

The Hebrew says, literally, that the king's sleep fled. The book gives no reason for it, and the silence invites the reader to ask who was behind it.

Persian kings kept official records, and the book refers to them several times. Greek historians describe the Persian custom of rewarding those who had served the king. That Mordecai's deed had gone unrewarded for about five years, from the king's seventh year to his twelfth, was a failure of royal honor that a king was bound to put right.

Nothing in the chapter is a miracle. A sleepless night, a passage read, a forgotten deed, and Haman arriving early, all within hours of Mordecai's planned death. Everything arrives exactly on time.
passages.later: The book's own record of the plot was written in chapter 2: ‘And all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king’ (2:23). A psalm speaks of the God of Israel who keeps watch: ‘Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep’ (Psalm 121:4).
passages.hard:
Is this chapter describing God's hand, or a string of lucky coincidences?

The text never says that God kept the king awake or guided the reading. A reader who does not believe in providence can read it as a well-made story of coincidence, and some modern scholars read the book mainly as a court tale about human wit and fortune.

But the crowding of coincidences is the point of the chapter: the sleepless night, the passage read, the unrewarded deed, and Haman's early arrival all come together within hours. Jewish and Christian readers have long taken this as the book's way of pointing to God without naming him, and even Haman's advisers sense, at the end of the chapter, that something more than chance is at work. The book leaves the reader to draw that conclusion rather than stating it, which is often how providence is known: clearly only looking back.
passages.asks: A record nobody remembered was read on exactly the right night. Ask where, looking back, you can see timing in your own life that you could not have arranged. And ask whether you can trust God's care in a night when you cannot sleep and nothing makes sense yet.

passages.t: The man the king delights to honor
passages.happening:
The king asks Haman, “What should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” Now Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?” (verse 6).

So Haman describes it: a royal robe that the king himself has worn, a horse the king has ridden with a royal crest on its head, and one of the king's noblest princes to lead the man through the city square, proclaiming before him that this is what is done for the man the king delights to honor (verses 7-9).

“Hurry,” said the king to Haman, “and do just as you proposed. Take the robe and the horse to Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate” (verse 10). And Haman does it, crying out before Mordecai the very words he had meant for himself (verse 11).

Mordecai goes back to the king's gate. ‘But Haman rushed home, with his head covered in grief’ (verse 12). His advisers and his wife tell him that if Mordecai is a Jew, he will not prevail against him, but will surely fall (verse 13). While they are still talking, the king's eunuchs arrive and hurry him to Esther's banquet (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Honor in the ancient world was public. To be honored was to be seen being honored. Haman asks for the most visible signs of royal favor: a robe the king himself had worn, which meant sharing in his dignity, and a horse the king had ridden. Joseph was honored in the same way in Egypt.

The narrator lets the reader hear Haman's private thought, so that his long, eager description of the honors he expects becomes painful to watch. The phrase the man whom the king is delighted to honor comes again and again, and it ends in Haman's own mouth as he proclaims it before Mordecai.

Haman goes home with his head covered, a sign of grief and shame. His advisers' warning uses the word fall twice. Many scholars see this chapter as the center of the book, with the events before it mirrored by the events after it: the proud man brought low, and the humble man raised up.
passages.later: Pharaoh honored Joseph in the same way in Egypt: ‘He had Joseph ride in his second chariot’ (Genesis 41:43). Mary's song praises the God who ‘has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble’ (Luke 1:52).
passages.asks: Haman thought the honor was for him, and he had to give it to the man he hated. Ask where you have assumed that you are the one who deserves notice. And ask whether you can rejoice when someone else is honored.
